report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced a sweeping set of "reciprocal" tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The announcement came with executive order and a chart.
Baseline tariff
A 10% tariff on imports from nearly all countries took effect April 5.
Higher country-specific rates
Countries with large trade surpluses with the US faced higher rates. These took effect April 9 and were described as roughly half of what those countries supposedly charged the US, based on a formula using trade deficits.
Examples:
China: 34%
Vietnam: 46%
Thailand: 36%
Taiwan: 32%
Switzerland: 31%
Indonesia: 32%
India: 26%
South Korea: 25%
Japan: 24%
European Union: 20%
Exemptions and exclusions
Canada and Mexico were not hit with the reciprocal tariffs. Their goods that comply with USMCA stayed under separate, earlier fentanyl- and border-related tariffs.
Goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs were excluded, including steel, aluminum and autos/auto parts.
Other exclusions included pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, lumber, copper, bullion and certain energy products.
What happened next
On April 9, Trump paused the higher country-specific rates for 90 days, leaving the 10% baseline in place. China was the exception. Escalating tit-for-tat increases pushed US tariffs on Chinese goods to 145% in total, including earlier tariffs.
Later in 2025, many of the country rates were replaced by negotiated deals and new executive orders. Courts also challenged the legal basis of the IEEPA tariffs.
I haven't checked the current status of these tariffs. They have changed a lot since April 2025, so I can look up where things stand now if you'd like.
